articles.title: LIV Golf is dead ... but it changed golf forever
articles.summary: LIV Golf has officially ceased operations, bringing an end to the most disruptive eras for any major American sport in decades.
articles.body:
LIV Golf was built on a foundation of defiance, greed, "grow the game" platitudes and — most significantly — unfathomable waves of money. But when the money ran dry, the defiance became an unsustainable strategy, the platitudes were as meaningless as a well-struck shot on a driving range.

LIV Golf has officially begun winding down via bankruptcy, bringing an end to the most disruptive era of any major American sport in decades. The final clear-the-course horn sounded in a New Jersey courtroom on Thursday morning after the league's would-be creditor declined to offer LIV a lifeline. The wind-down process designed to address the demands of the league's creditors will begin in the coming days.

BC Partners Credit, which had reached a tentative agreement to fund "LIV 2.0" with up to $300 million, withdrew that offer after LIV was unable to convince enough big-name players to sign on . Jon Rahm, Sergio Garcia, Graeme McDowell and numerous others decided not to follow LIV into its next iteration; Brooks Koepka and Patrick Reed had already cut ties after their contracts ran out.

The Financial Times reported that about 30 players had committed to the league's new vision, a global, player-owned golf tour, with another 10 players — including some star names — on the fence about joining. But that apparently wasn't sufficient for BC, which determined the league was no longer a viable operation.

The breakaway golf series, initially funded by Saudi billions, altered the entire trajectory of golf, drawing battle lines between colleagues, injecting billions into the sport, increasing purses, changing the makeups of the Ryder Cup and all four majors, and, eventually, reshaping the PGA Tour's entire schedule. But after Saudi Arabia withdrew its financial backing, LIV Golf simply couldn't continue as an independent operation in the high-stakes, high-cost world it had helped create.

LIV Golf took the sport on a wild, expensive ride, one that fundamentally altered every element of the game. Its impact on golf, as a sport and as an institution, will last long after anyone remembers what a "Range Goat" was, but not in the way its founders intended.

Truthfully, with its rebellious, in-your-face, golf-but-louder origins, LIV Golf was always doomed right from the start. Golf as a pursuit is intensely individual, golf as a sport is overwhelmingly personality driven, but golf as a business is, and has always been, an establishment, risk-averse, lower-case-c conservative operation.

So when LIV Golf — funded by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, personified by noted provocateur Greg Norman — thundered into the golf world in 2021, it hit like a bowling ball thrown on a table of pimento cheese sandwiches. Limitless money! Chill attitudes! Live music! So much money! Dance parties! Neon everywhere! And did we mention the money?

The LIV plane almost never made it off the runway. Phil Mickelson gave away the entire game in late 2021, declaring that he was willing to go into business with the "scary motherf******" — a phrase that now lives in golf infamy — of Saudi Arabia to take a bite out of the PGA Tour's imperial dominance of the game. After considerable PR damage control, and more shovelfuls of Saudi riches, LIV began playing tournaments in 2022 with a distinctive roster of players.

LIV's value proposition — sure, stick it to the man, whatever, but mostly the money — attracted many of golf's most notable antagonists, along with known but past-their-prime stars drawn by a payday impossible to achieve anywhere else on earth. Dustin Johnson, Bryson DeChambeau, Brooks Koepka, Patrick Reed, Ian Poulter, Lee Westwood — each did the same performative "I have no comment" dance before acknowledging that, yes, they would be taking an eight- or nine-figure payday to jump to LIV.

In LIV's earliest days, the breakaway circuit's Saudi backing generated the most heat, with critics pointing to Saudi Arabia's horrific human rights record. Players drew criticism from 9/11 remembrance organizations, and fumbled their justifications for taking Saudi money in cinematic ways. LIV was a prime example of sportswashing, using soft-power initiatives like sports to help scrub the image of the autocratic petrostate.

And for a short while, it worked. With rare exception, LIV didn't exactly draw massive crowds, either in person or on television. But the boundless wealth of the Saudi regime behind LIV was enough to catch the PGA Tour's attention. Then-PGA Tour CEO Jay Monahan and Rory McIlroy, among others, framed the distinction between the two tours in moral terms, between tradition and short-term gain, between legacy and blood money. Lawsuits and accusations between the two tours flew, forcing everyone involved to pick a side.

However, the truth was far more complicated, and the moral stances far more fragile. The Tour realized that it was being drawn into an unsustainable financial arms race, and in June 2023, the PGA Tour and the Saudi PIF announced a cessation of legal hostilities and a "framework agreement" for future cooperation between the two.

The framework agreement caught the entire golf world by surprise. The fact that the framework agreement amounted to absolutely nothing, however, did not. The PGA Tour went ahead and sought outside investment to reduce its potential reliance on the PIF; LIV Golf went ahead and poached several players, most notably then-world No. 3 Jon Rahm, with hints that more defections were soon to come.

Even as LIV continued to make steps toward legitimacy — Koepka had won the 2023 PGA Championship while a member of LIV, and DeChambeau captured the 2024 U.S. Open, and the majors agreed to extend limited invitations to LIV members — the breakaway tour couldn't get traction in the United States. Events in both South Africa and Australia drew significant crowds, suggesting there was an unmet hunger for tournament golf in those nations. But stateside, LIV events dwindled toward irrelevance.

Through 2024 and 2025, some signs of hope emerged for LIV and its advocates. The Official World Golf Rankings agreed to give ranking points to certain LIV players, offering them a pathway back into the majors. And earlier this year, Augusta National chairman Fred Ridley thanked LIV by name in his closing remarks, an indication of the perch that the tour had ascended.

But at the same time, there were troubling signs. Just before the holidays in late 2025, Koepka began pursuing a path back onto the PGA Tour, and Reed followed soon afterward. The Tour offered a one-time-only pathway back for certain notable LIV members — Rahm and DeChambeau in particular — but no other player followed.

Then, in April of this year, the hammer dropped. Just days after the end of the Masters, the PIF announced it would be pulling all funding from LIV, effective at the end of this season. The move came as a total shock to LIV officials, who were forced to scramble for potential investment to keep operating as a leaner, less-flush organization.

And the hits kept coming. Neither Rahm nor DeChambeau seemed publicly thrilled with the state of affairs at LIV. Although DeChambeau got involved with discussions with outside investors, he's also a free agent and untethered contractually to LIV Golf. When the Saudis' wealth vanished, so too did his leverage and his incentive to stay with LIV. The cancellation of one summer tournament under dubious circumstances, the mounting small-scale lawsuits, and the conspicuous lack of investor announcements all combined to darken the clouds over LIV.

Late in July, Cleeks captain Martin Kaymer indicated that there were serious concerns about whether the tournament's season-ending championship would even happen at all. More ominously, the Asian Tour, which had been aligned with LIV, entered into a long-term agreement with the PGA and European tours , effectively cutting LIV out of the international tournament circuit.

Although LIV had sought to employ an open-door policy — its players could play on other tours in addition to their LIV commitments — the other tours didn't reciprocate. The PGA Tour had a longstanding suspension in place for any player who teed it up in a LIV event, and when the DP World Tour also blocked LIV players from its tournaments in October, LIV lost yet another perk for its players.

From there, it was only a matter of time.

So what did LIV Golf bring to the game, and how did LIV change the game?

The circuit's "Golf, But Louder" slogan never really stuck; turns out that most galleries and TV viewers prefer golf tournaments that focus on actual golf, not a Chainsmokers concert or a petting zoo. On a broader scale, LIV's emergence turned golf into a cold, bloody pursuit of money, with tournaments and tours alike touting the massive sizes of their purses … which was good news for the players, not so much for the fans.

More broadly, LIV forced the PGA Tour to take a hard look at how it's done business for the past 50-plus years. The result: an entirely new PGA Tour schedule with two different tracks of players, "champions" and "challengers." The best and most notable players will definitely benefit from this new framework that begins in 2028, the lower-ranked ones, probably not.

On a less-mercenary note, LIV's greatest legacy is that it demonstrated there's interest in golf far beyond the traditional American-European axis. LIV events in the Southern Hemisphere topped six figures in attendance; any tour that's able to meet that need will surely thrive.

LIV Golf enriched players and destroyed reputations, forcing new perspectives on the game at great cost. It's definitive proof that creating a legitimate rival sports league at this point in the industry's growth is effectively impossible. It laid bare the mercenary soul at the heart of the sport. It deprived certain players of prime competitive years on the PGA Tour, but also made those players astronomically wealthy.

For years to come, LIV will be a case study in hubris and ambition, the power of wealth against the power of legacy. In the end, legacy won out … though not before millions were earned, and billions were spent. Golf is quieter now, but forever changed.

articles.title: LIV and Let Die: Rival League Tells Bankruptcy Court It Will Wind Down Operations
articles.summary: LIV Golf is shuttering after five years that fractured the sport's landscape with promise of Saudi riches, announcing Thursday in bankruptcy court it plans to wind down operations instead of launching a new version because it didn't have enough support.
articles.body:
LIV Golf is shuttering after five years that fractured the sport's landscape with promise of Saudi riches, announcing Thursday in bankruptcy court it plans to wind down operations instead of launching a new version because it didn't have enough support.

"The debtors are not currently proceeding with the LIV 2.0 plan," attorney Matthew Williams of Gibson Dunn said in a hearing in New Jersey. "Instead, the debtors are toggling to a value-maximizing wind-down in their business."

LIV Golf, which launched in June 2022 by offering nine-figure signing bonuses to lure top names away from the PGA Tour, lost Saudi Arabia funding in April after spending more than $5 billion.

It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Sept. 8 and thought it had a lifeline in BC Partners Credit, which pledged a $300 million investment to pivot to a more financially sustainable "LIV 2.0." But players like Jon Rahm and Sergio Garcia, Tyrrell Hatton and Louis Oosthuizen, weren't interested.

"BC Partners Credit supported a transaction that aligned the interests of players and investors, offering a credible path toward building a sustainable future for LIV Golf," BC Partners said in a statement. "While there was great support for the league, we are disappointed that mutually acceptable terms could not be reached among the various stakeholders."

Instead of planning for a new version for 2027, LIV enters a liquidation phase.

Rahm already agreed to forfeit all claims against LIV — said to be worth some $100 million — to get out of his contract. He is back to playing the European tour, with hopes there will be a path back to the PGA Tour. The tour currently has a one-year ban dating to players' last LIV appearance.

LIV Golf paid $15.6 million to retain seven of its executives , including $6.375 million to CEO Scott O'Neil, in the months between the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia and LIV filing for bankruptcy. Those payments are not unusual for a company trying to emerge from bankruptcy. The question now is whether those payments can be voided since LIV isn't going forward.

"Building a global platform designed to bring new, younger, and more diverse fans to the sport of golf has been the round of a lifetime for all of us," said Scott O'Neil, the CEO of LIV who took over from Greg Norman at the start of 2025.

"LIV Golf was fun, demanding, inspiring, at times challenging — but always rewarding."

LIV suffered a number of setbacks this year, none bigger than losing its source of its money when PIF changed its investment strategy and said it would no longer pay for the league at the conclusion of its fifth season.

The Asian Tour, which received financial support from LIV for an International Series, decided in July to renew an alliance with the PGA Tour and the commercially known DP World Tour in Europe.

And as the league was trying to pivot to LIV 2.0, European tour CEO Guy Kinnings last month said anyone signing up for LIV need not apply for membership on the European tour, which put European players at risk of having no part in the Ryder Cup.

Kinnings said in an interview with The Scotsman newspaper earlier this week, "But we also have to protect the tour against an entity who spent, so we are told, over $7 billion, with one of their aims being to 'destroy the DP World Tour.'"

LIV was originally run by Norman, who tried unsuccessfully to start a world tour in 1994 only to have it quashed by Arnold Palmer and the PGA Tour. Norman had Saudi money at his disposal, and promoted LIV as "Golf, but louder" with its blaring music, 54-hole shotgun starts and $25 million in prize funds — individual and team — at each event.

But it had no broadcast deal the first year, meaning it had to cover production costs. It got the CW Network in 2023, and eventually got Fox Sports to sign on in 2025.

Key to a new version of LIV was a "critical mass" of players to stick around, and BC Partners extended the Oct. 25 deadline. This was more about names than numbers, ultimately, and it couldn't reach agreement with enough players.

"Ultimately, despite everyone's best efforts, we just couldn't get to the level of combined financial and player support necessary for a viable LIV 2.0 within the required timeline," Williams said.

In the end, LIV held 62 tournaments on every continent golf is played except for South America. It had a feel-good moment in Australia this year when Anthony Kim returned from a 12-year hiatus of addiction to win again. Bryson DeChambeau shot a 58. Joaquin Niemann won seven times.

They are part of a short history, and now have to find a way back.

Brooks Koepka was the first to return. The five-time major champion got out of his LIV deal with one year remaining, and the PGA Tour created a path — with financial penalties — to return. Patrick Reed chose not to extend his deal in January and now is poised to return to the PGA Tour next year through his performance in Europe.

Rahm had said on Tuesday he would be willing to pay the same price as Koepka, though it was unlikely that same deal would be offered.
authors: Doug Ferguson and Stephen Whyno, Associated Press

articles.title: LIV Golf bankruptcy hearing: League scraps plans to launch 'LIV 2.0' and 'winding down operations' after losing funding
articles.summary: LIV Golf was unable to secure fresh investment to relaunch in 2027; BC Partners cancelled their plan to potentially finance the circuit into next season, following a mass exodus of high-profile players that included Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and Sergio Garcia
articles.body:
A lawyer representing the organisation announced the decision in a bankruptcy court hearing on Thursday in New Jersey, ending months of speculation over LIV Golf's future in the men's game.

"The debtors were ultimately unable to bring the key parties to a fully consensual arrangement that would have supported a financially viable LIV 2.0 league," Gibson Dunn partner Matthew Williams, one of LIV's attorneys, said.

"As a result, the debtors are not currently proceeding with the LIV 2.0 plan. Instead, the debtors are toggling to a value-maximising wind down of their business."

The Financial Times first reported on Wednesday that BC Partners Credit, who had been lined up as potential backers following the withdrawal of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund in April, had pulled out of a deal worth more than $300m (£220m).

LIV Golf had been forced to apply for Chapter 11 bankruptcy after the 2026 season, effectively cancelling playing contracts, with three-time champion Jon Rahm among the initial high-profile departures.

Sergio Garcia, Ian Poulter, Tyrrell Hatton, Louis Oosthuizen and Lee Westwood had already confirmed their intentions not to continue with LIV Golf, prior to the confirmation that the circuit would not continue.

In a statement, LIV Golf said: "Since April 2026, the league's leadership team, with the support of its independent directors and advisors, has run a disciplined and thorough process to identify the best, value-maximising path forward for the company and its stakeholders.

"Despite extensive discussions, the relevant parties were ultimately unable to reach a consensual resolution of certain outstanding terms of the transaction contemplated by the Restructuring Support Agreement (RSA). As a result, the RSA has been terminated, and the transaction is not expected to move forward at this time."

'At times challenging but always rewarding' - LIV Golf chief reflects on legacy

The league was originally run by Greg Norman and launched as an Invitational Series in 2022, with the circuit growing over the following seasons to secure Official World Golf Ranking points and player pathways to majors.

Brooks Koepka got out of his deal ahead of the 2026 season and the PGA Tour created a path - with financial penalties - to return, while Patrick Reed chose not to renew his contract and is now set to return to the PGA Tour via his DP World Tour performances.

The DP World Tour said in September that any player who signed with LIV 2.0 would be denied membership on its circuit, with its chief executive Guy Kinnings and Rory McIlroy both saying that LIV Golf was trying to 'destroy the European Tour'.

Only a handful of players, including Brendan Steele and Cameron Tringale, had publicly stated their support for the new format, with BC Partners "disappointed" that "mutually acceptable terms could not be reached" to proceed with the circuit.

LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil said: "LIV Golf was fun, demanding, inspiring, at times challenging - but always rewarding. Building a global platform designed to bring new, younger, and more diverse fans to the sport of golf has been the round of a lifetime for all of us.

"We created memories that I hope will inspire a new generation of fans to follow, play, and fall in love with this great game.

"Golf has given so much to so many, and my hope is that those entrusted with its future will lead with the generosity, perspective, and shared purpose this extraordinary game deserves."

The end of the road for LIV - what next for its players?

"The writing was on the wall when the Saudis withdrew their funding back in April and the league filed for bankruptcy in September, but there was still a determination - with fresh investment - to persevere with the so-called LIV 2.0.

"Recent weeks have seen a succession of high-profile names announce they wouldn't be committing to this newest version of the league. With BC Partners also no longer proceeding, LIV Golf was left with no other option than to officially wind down the league and liquidate its assets.

"Where does that leave the players? The PGA Tour has been consistent in saying players will have to serve a one-year suspension from the date of their last event - that was in August. That leaves the DP World Tour as the most desirable option for many - with a mid-November deadline to take up membership, if eligible.

"The likes of Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and Sergio Garcia have already said that's where they'll be playing, while veterans like Lee Westwood or Paul Casey could re-join the DP World Tour - following tournament suspensions - due to career money list exemptions. For others, it's more complicated.

"Bryson DeChambeau, who was fully committed to LIV 2.0, has just one year remaining of his option to take up DP World Tour membership, but that's not an option for other past major champions like Cameron Smith or Dustin Johnson.

"Players who would add value to events could be given tournament invites, but even then these are unlikely to be extended to the premiere events. The PGA Tour is also going through its own changes, with it still unclear whether 10 cards will be on offer through the DP World Tour at the end of 2027.

"For many, the pathway back to the top could be a long and tricky one."

Watch the PGA Tour, DP World Tour, LPGA Tour, majors and more live on Sky Sports. Get the latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract .

articles.title: LIV Golf winding down operations, lawyer says in bankruptcy hearing
articles.summary: LIV Golf is winding down operations instead of launching a new version because of a lack of financial support.
articles.body: LIV Golf is winding down operations instead of launching a new version because of a lack of financial support. A lawyer representing the organization announced the decision in a bankruptcy court hearing Thursday in New Jersey. “The debtors are not currently proceeding with the LIV 2.0 plan,” Matthew Williams of Gibson Dunn said. “Instead, the debtors are toggling to a value-maximizing wind-down in their business.” LIV Golf lost Saudi Arabia funding in April after having spent more than $5 billion since 2022. LIV filed for bankruptcy in September. Since announcing plans for a new version, top players like Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton have bailed. The league was originally run by Greg Norman. A few months after the start of the Iran war, PIF changed its investment strategy in April and said it would no longer pay for LIV Golf after the 2026 season. The Asian Tour, which received a financial boost from LIV for an International Series, decided in July to renew an alliance with the PGA Tour and European tour. And as LIV was trying to emerge from bankruptcy, filed on September 8, the European tour laid down a crushing ultimatum by saying anyone who signed with LIV 2.0 need not apply for membership in the commercially known DP World Tour. That would make European players ineligible for the Ryder Cup. Guy Kinnings, the European tour CEO, called out LIV in an interview with The Scotsman when he said, “But we also have to protect the tour against an entity who spent, so we are told, over $7 billion, with one of their aims being to ‘destroy the DP World Tour.’” Rahm, Sergio Garcia, Louis Oosthuizen and Tyrrell Hatton also said they would no longer stay with LIV, and the rival league also lost young players like David Puig of Spain and Tom McKibbin of Northern Ireland. The year began with Brooks Koepka getting out of his LIV deal with one year remaining, and the PGA Tour created a path – with financial penalties – to return. Patrick Reed chose not to extend his deal and now is poised to return to the PGA Tour next year through his performance in Europe. Rahm had said on Tuesday he would be willing to pay the same price as Koepka, though it was unlikely that same deal would be offered. LIV 2.0 was pushing player equity and prize money that was more than half the $20 million purses for individuals when it began in 2022. LIV’s final event was in August in Indianapolis, won by Michael La Sasso. He failed to get through the second stage of European tour Q-school last week.

articles.title: Penalizan a McIlroy con dos golpes y todos se acuerdan de sus duras críticas a DeChambeau en el British
articles.standfirst: El norirlandés fue penalizado por mejorar la situación de su bola durante la primera ronda del Abu Dhabi Championship, como el 'Científico' en Royal Birkdale
articles.summary: El norirlandés fue penalizado por mejorar la situación de su bola durante la primera ronda del Abu Dhabi Championship, como el 'Científico' en Royal Birkdale
articles.body: El destino es a veces caprichoso y Rory McIlroy recibió una penalización de dos golpes durante la primera ronda del Abu Dhabi Championship este jueves. El único error en la tarjeta del norirlandés fue un doble bogey en el hoyo 12 (par 4) de Yas Links. Sin embargo, posteriormente, este doble bogey se convirtió en un cuádruple bogey, tras recibir una penalización de dos golpes. El campeón del Masters fue penalizado tras considerarse que había infringido la regla 8.1 al presionar con su palo el césped situado detrás de su bola. Había intentado un chip que retrocedió y acto seguido parece que quiso comprobar la profundidad de la bola apoyando el palo justo por delante de la misma. Se considera que mejoró la situación de su bola. El número 2 del mundo se enteró de esta circunstancia después de su ronda, y tras conversar con los oficiales del torneo y sus dos compañeros de partido, Patrick Reed y Eugenio Chacarra, se le impuso una penalización. Rory comentó que le mostraron la acción en un vídeo: “Hice mi primer approach desde la parte baja de la loma, no se elevó, volvió a bajar y rodó hasta un hoyo, y luego, mientras intentaba tantear la posición de la bola, en el primer plano de la cámara se puede ver como un pequeño trozo de hierba alrededor del hoyo baja cuando pongo el palo detrás de la bola. Supongo que el césped no vuelve a su posición original. Obviamente no hay mala intención. Juego según las reglas, intento hacer todo lo posible para no acabar nunca en estas situaciones, pero viendo el vídeo, no tiene muy buena pinta”. McIlroy añadió a su explicación: “Obviamente esa no era mi intención, solo estoy tratando de sentir la posición de la bola, está en el fondo de un hoyo arenoso, estoy tratando de sentir si puedo darle un golpe de 54 grados a la parte posterior de la bola, pero en el proceso, este trozo de césped se ha ido aplastando”. El pasado verano, durante el British Open, Bryson DeChambeau también fue sancionado con dos golpes por mejorar la situación de su bola. No era exactamente el mismo caso, pero el ‘Científico’, que estaba en la pelea por el torneo, defendió su inocencia y Rory fue muy drástico con él: “Sí, creo que no hay duda de que mejoró la línea de su swing. De nuevo, da igual si fue por descuido o intencional (si así fuera lo podrían haber expulsado), creo que no importa. Ojalá haya sido por descuido, pero creo que la penalización de dos golpes estuvo totalmente justificada”.

articles.title: Tiger Woods' Potential PGA Tour Champions Future Discussed By Alker, 'He Wants to Add to His Tally'
articles.summary: Tiger Woods has yet to announce if and when he'll return to professional golf, but it appears the 50-year-old is making progress towards playing the PGA Tour Champions.
articles.body:
Tiger Woods has yet to announce if and when he'll return to professional golf, but it appears the 50-year-old is making progress towards playing the PGA Tour Champions.

Two-time Charles Schwab Cup champion Steven Alker said Woods has had "talk" with other PGA Tour Champions players about Woods joining the circuit.

"This talk, yeah, he seriously wants to come out, there's inside talking," Alker told Golfweek's Todd Kelly (h/t Heavy's Henry DiGennaro ). "He wants to come out and play, and in particular, I think the big events, like the invitationals or Stricker's event and the Furyk event. He's got his buddies who really him to do their events. You got the USGA, you got the U.S. Senior Open. He wants to add to his tally, you know? "I seriously think he'll come out if he gets fit and in the right mind."

Breece Deactivates Twitter After Threats

While there's no timeline for Woods' PGA Tour or Tour Champions' return, he is "expected" to play for the Jupiter Links Golf Club in the Dec. 27 opener of TGL's third season, according to ESPN's Mark Schlabach .

Woods played in just one GL match last season because of back surgery. He hasn't appeared in a PGA Tour event since 2024.

articles.title: Hunter Henry’s practice absence will concern Patriots fans ahead of Packers clash
articles.summary: Hunter Henry hasn’t made progress in his injury recovery, presenting question marks for the New England Patriots ahead of their Week 9 matchup this weekend....
articles.body:
Hunter Henry hasn't made progress in his injury recovery, presenting question marks for the New England Patriots ahead of their Week 9 matchup this weekend.

Henry has been playing in the NFL since 2016, going through his sixth season with the Patriots. He stands out as one of the better veteran tight ends in the league, helping New England make a deep playoff run to Super Bowl 60 last season.

However, Henry suffered a foot injury during the Patriots' win over the Miami Dolphins in Week 8. It has impacted him enough to the point that he has been absent from practices for two consecutive days , per reporter Mike Reiss.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

"TE Hunter Henry, who was limited to eight snaps Sunday after injuring his foot, is absent from practice for the second day in a row," Reiss wrote on Thursday.

What lies ahead for Hunter Henry, Patriots

It is tough news for the Patriots to get regarding Hunter Henry. They await his full recovery from the foot injury, looking to other options if he isn't ready for Week 9.

Henry has settled in as one of Drake Maye's top targets, having reached 85 targets, 60 catches and 650 yards each of the past two seasons. This year, he has caught 29 passes for 326 yards and two touchdowns in a balanced New England attack.

New England has a 5-3 record this season, sitting at second place in the AFC East Division standings. They are above the New York Jets and the Miami Dolphins while trailing the Buffalo Bills. In terms of the conference standings, they are seventh place. They lead over the Cleveland Browns and the Las Vegas Raiders while being under the Cincinnati Bengals and the Kansas City Chiefs.

The Patriots will continue preparations for their upcoming matchup this weekend, being at home. They host the Green Bay Packers in Week 9 as kickoff commences on Nov. 8 at 4:25 p.m. ET.
